title: Choose a Cato
hookLine: pick someone good and live as if they were watching

cards: When you're stuck on something, a hard conversation, a temptation, a choice at work, there's a question people reach for: what would she do? My grandmother. My old coach.
The best boss I ever had. Some people keep a name on a bracelet for just that moment. The move is old.
Yesterday Seneca said to live as if God saw you. In his eleventh letter he makes it more human and more specific, with advice borrowed, once again, from Epicurus.

teach.b: The letter starts with a young friend of Lucilius who blushed while talking to Seneca. Seneca liked him for it. Blushing is natural, he says, and no amount of wisdom removes it.
Actors can fake tears or fear on stage, but they can't blush on command. Some things in us we can't control; character is about what we do with the rest. Then the advice.

teach.h: KEEP A GOOD PERSON BEFORE YOU.
teach.b: Epicurus told his students to pick a person of good character and keep them always before their eyes, living as if that person were watching and acting as if that person could see.
A guardian, Seneca calls it, a witness you carry with you. Choose a Cato, he says. Cato the Younger was the stern Roman Stoic who refused to bend to Julius Caesar and died rather than submit.
If Cato feels too severe, choose Laelius, a gentler man, a statesman known as the Wise. Choose someone whose life, words and even face have pleased you. Why does it work?

teach.h: NO STRAIGHT LINE WITHOUT A RULER.
teach.b: You can't straighten something crooked without a ruler. We need a measure outside ourselves to see where we bend.

Your Cato doesn't have to be well-known, or Roman, or even alive: a grandmother, a saint, a teacher, a neighbor. Just someone whose goodness you're sure of, and whose imagined gaze makes you stand a little straighter.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism keep a chosen model in mind, a person of good character, and ask in hard moments what that person would see in their choices.

the watcher idea comes from Epicurus
Seneca credits him: keep a good person before your eyes, as if they could see.
your Cato has to be a well-known Roman
Seneca says choose anyone whose life and words you admire; Laelius is offered as a gentler option.

games.q: Seneca tells you to choose Cato as your watcher. but Cato feels far too stern for you. what does Seneca say?
o: too bad: Cato or no one.
then choose Laelius, a gentler man.
then you don't need a watcher.
games.why: he offers Laelius as a gentler model: the point is someone whose goodness you trust, not the strictest one available.

practice: Let faces come to mind, people whose goodness you trust, living or gone, well-known or known only to you, and let one step forward. Recall one small, straight thing they actually did.
Hold it like a ruler beside one choice you're facing, and simply measure, no scolding.

wordCard.voice: Cato. Seneca's eleventh letter, borrowing from Epicurus: choose someone good and live as if they were watching, a ruler to straighten yourself against. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: so choose a Cato, from Seneca's eleventh letter.

carryVoice: Your line: stand a little straighter. A good witness goes wherever you go. Until tomorrow.
